zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The returned transcription and review notes are separate scan-based work, not a reproduction of that index.

runs.text: Item, Qualquer couſa de apetite quando ſe

lines.note: This continues Sacana from the preceding page with another sense: an appetizing food eaten in connection with drinking. Item is printed in full here.
The food is eaten so that one may drink afterward or with it. This completes the broader drinking-accompaniment sense, rather than restricting Sacana to fish.
Sacanna describes something flourishing, prosperous, or vigorous. Prospera is a continuous printed word, correcting the draft's artificial split pros pera; its short s is retained.
The definition continues with being in full vigor. The Japanese example begins a phrase for a person in the prime of life, with fito divided at the margin.

runs.text: Homem que eſta naflor da idade.

lines.note: To completes fito. The Portuguese describes a man in the flower of his age; the scan reads flor, not fior, while the tightly set naflor is retained.
The example describes being at the height of power or prosperity. The printed joining naforça is preserved instead of silently regularizing the Portuguese spacing.
Prosperity and favorable circumstances complete the gloss of the preceding Japanese example. Bonança here describes good fortune rather than a literal calm at sea.
Sacanobori means ascending against a river's current. The historical principal parts and the printed line-end division da-/goa are retained.

runs.text: goa em algum rio, ou correrem as agoas pera

lines.note: The gloss covers both traveling upriver and the water itself flowing upward. Agoa retains the dictionary's spelling, here divided after the preceding da-.

runs.text: cima com a força da marẽ, &c.

lines.note: The water can run upstream under tidal pressure. The draft's marẽ is retained: the small, thickened mark is ambiguous between a nasal mark and an accent, so its precise shape remains uncertain.

runs.text: Sacaqi. i, Camino mayeni tatçuru qi.

lines.note: Sacaqi is explained in Japanese as a tree set before a deity. The synonym phrase is roman, while Hũ begins the Portuguese definition without expanding its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: pao, ou aruore q̃ ſe aleuanta, ou planta diãte

lines.note: The Portuguese describes a piece of timber or tree raised or planted before a sacred place. The abbreviated q̃ and diãte remain literal.

runs.text: dos Camis, ou diante deſua ermida.

lines.note: The location is before the Camis or their shrine. Camis is embedded in the Portuguese explanation; enlargement supports retaining the draft's tightly set deſua rather than adding a word space.
Sacari is the strength or prime condition of something. The gloss introduces examples of this peak or full-vigor sense rather than the separate animal-heat entry below.
Fana zacari and fanano ſacari name the height of flowering. The alternative is introduced by the roman l, and the first form's printed word separation is retained.

runs.text: em que eſtão em ſeu vigor as roſas, ou flores.

lines.note: The Portuguese defines the time when roses or flowers are in full bloom. This completes the botanical example of Sacari.
A visible paragraph mark introduces Toxino ſacari, the prime of life; it was omitted from the draft. The Portuguese's tightly set daida- continues as de below.
This finishes idade and closes the preceding example with &c. The final abbreviation contains c, correcting the draft's &e without joining the physical lines.

runs.text: Vir, ou ſer o tempo do cio dos

lines.note: This verbal entry concerns animals coming into heat. Its printed principal parts include ru, unlike the abbreviated neighboring entry below.
Necoga ſacaru illustrates a cat being in heat. The visible terminal mark after o is retained even though it falls after the Portuguese article.
The cat example ends with com ocio, meaning being in heat in this context. The draft's joined spacing is retained; it is not interpreted as idleness.
This entry describes an unpleasant astringent sensation in the mouth. The scan really prints the abbreviated second principal part u; no expected r is supplied.

runs.text: tir a boca desabrida, & com desſabor dalgũa

lines.note: The mouth feels unpleasant or ill-tasting. Desabrida has a visible short s, correcting the draft's r; the neighboring mixed short-s/long-s spelling desſabor is preserved.
The sensation is attributed to something sour that one eats. This closes the mouth-related sense and distinguishes it from the preceding animal-heat sense.
Sacaſama and Sacaſamani describe reversal or an upside-down orientation. The adverb label Adu. belongs to the italic Portuguese apparatus; the alternative forms remain roman.

runs.text: ou às aueßas, ou cabeça abaixo.

lines.note: The alternatives mean the wrong way round or head downward. The printed double-s form in aueßas is retained rather than expanded or modernized.
Sacatçubo denotes a wine jar or pot. Iarra preserves the printed initial I used where modern Portuguese writes J, and boyão is not normalized.

runs.text: O que ſe paga pollo vinho.

lines.note: This Sacate is the money paid for wine. It is a distinct sense from the reversed handgrip introduced in the next entry.

runs.text: O tomar algũa couſa na mão ao modo

lines.note: The second Sacate describes holding something in the hand in a particular reversed grip. The explanatory comparison with a dagger follows on the next line.
The grip is likened to grasping a dagger for stabbing. Vaqizaxiuo begins the Japanese example, with the object marker joined as printed.
The example means drawing the short sword with this reversed grip. The Portuguese word maneira continues below, but no terminal hyphen is visible after ma.

runs.text: neira como quem quer dar de punhaladas.

lines.note: The grip is described as that of someone about to deliver dagger thrusts. This completes maneira and the example without changing the physical line division.

runs.text: P. Batendo as palmas rogar pragas.

lines.note: Sacate vtçu is explained as clapping the hands while uttering curses. P. introduces the poetic-use explanation and is italic here, not a detached roman terminal label.

runs.text: Certo vaſo como tina ou barça pe-

lines.note: Saca uoqe names a vessel for wine, compared with a tub or similar container. The printed separation within the Japanese headword is retained.
This finishes pera and identifies the vessel's use for wine. The short physical continuation belongs to Saca uoqe, not to the adjective below.
Sacaxij is first glossed as vigorous, healthy, and strong. Its next sense is explicitly regional and should not replace this initial physical-strength meaning.

runs.text: ¶ Item, No Cami he o meſmo q̃ Caxicoi, pru-

lines.note: In the Cami region the word is said to mean Caxicoi, clever or prudent. Both Japanese terms occur within the Portuguese explanation and retain its visible italic setting.
The regional gloss ends with prudent and sagacious. Dente completes the divided prudente rather than constituting a separate word or entry.
This is the nominal derivative of Sacaxij, expressing the corresponding quality. Its separate indented physical line and roman type are preserved.
This is the corresponding adverbial form. The visible caron over u is retained, rather than substituted with a circumflex or modern long-vowel notation.
Sacaxira is equated with Nacagoto and introduced as discord or ill will. The synonym after i, is an independent Japanese expression, not an embedded Portuguese term.

runs.text: mal querença que hum cauſa entre outros. Vt,

lines.note: The discord is specifically that which someone causes between other people. The two-word spelling mal querença is preserved before the example marker.
The example means sowing discord. The Japanese object phrase remains joined as printed, and yǔ retains its caron.

runs.text: Adega, ou tauerna, & caſa onde ſe faz,

lines.note: Sacaya can be a wine storehouse, tavern, or establishment where wine is made. The Portuguese uses vinho for the local alcoholic drink without requiring a grape-wine identification.
Selling wine completes the alternative functions of a Sacaya. This continuation belongs to the shop or brewery entry, not to the following anatomical headword.

runs.text: Parte da cabeça tirando as fontes,

lines.note: Sacayaqi names the head area excluding the temples, with another excluded part following below. The faint final letters of the headword agree with its repeated examples.
The nape is also excluded, and the example means shaving this part of the head. Sacayaqiuo replaces the draft's Sacayaqico; its worn u is supported by the clear repetition in the next column.

runs.text: esta parte da cabeça, ſ. moleira, & cucuruta.

lines.note: The shaving example continues from the left column, specifying the crown or top of the head. The explanatory abbreviation ſ. and the historical term cucuruta remain literal.
Toru and nuqu provide alternative verbs for removing the hair. The scan has roman l. nuqu, not the draft's I-nuqu; Arrencar retains its printed vowel.

runs.text: os cabelos deſta parte da cabeça como cuſtuma-

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies plucking hair from this part of the head. The statement about an earlier custom continues across the visible cuſtuma- division.
This completes the explanation that people formerly plucked the hair in this way. The dictionary's past-tense ending and spelling are not modernized.
This Sacaye means flourishing, initially of trees and vegetation. The plural Portuguese construction begins with trees and continues with herbs or grasses.
The plants are green and vigorous. A new paragraph introduces a metaphorical extension; the line-end hyphen after per is visible and retained.
The figurative sense is prospering, illustrated by flourishing in power or status. The print divides Estar as Es-/tar, retaining the short s of the draft.
The first example means being prosperous and powerful. A second begins Tomi ſacayuru, flourishing in wealth, with the Japanese verb divided at the margin.
This completes the example of flourishing in riches. Florecer is retained with one sibilant-free stem as printed, rather than modernized to florescer.

A separate Sacaye entry concerns intervening in a fight, with Toriſacayuru preferred. Meliùs is italic editorial language; the complete Im- of Impedir is also italic, correcting the split font assignment.
The gloss means preventing or separating people who are fighting. The line is physically indented, correcting its placement in the draft; the tightly printed apartaraos remains unchanged.
Sacayuqi describes continuing to flourish or prosper. The scan supports florecendo, correcting the draft's flarecendo, while the abbreviated principal part u is preserved.
The example speaks of the realm or reign continuing to flourish. The Portuguese begins with expansion and completes the prosperity sense on the next line.
The empire's prosperity completes the preceding example. The sentence remains a continuation, not a new entry or independent assertion about a historical ruler.
Sacazzuqi denotes a cup or drinking vessel. The example repeats the headword across the physical Sacazzu-/qi division, which is not silently joined.
Tilting the cup is equated with Nomu, to drink. The separator after i has a visible comma tail, correcting the draft's period; the Japanese synonym remains roman.
The Portuguese says to drink from the Sacazzuqui, retaining this embedded spelling with qui rather than the headword's qi. The separate S. label is roman.
Sacoſo is glossed as probably so, or in that manner. The adverb label and explanation are italic, while the headword is roman.
The example concerns the sorrow of parting. The marked final vowel of nagoriuoxǔ is u with a caron, not the draft's i; the compound verb continues below.
Rǒ completes the preceding divided Japanese verb. Mon. is a roman citation label, followed by a Portuguese translation expressing an inference and then a contrast.
The gloss says that there must have been longing or regret, but leaves the contrast abbreviated with &c. No missing conclusion is supplied.

runs.text: Couſa de engenho como dito ſutil, &c.

lines.note: This Sacu is an ingenious production, such as a clever saying. The following example illustrates an invention or remark devised by the speaker.
The speaker proposes to utter one ingenious saying. The future-intention form iuǒzu and the attached object marker are retained; Mon. is a separate citation label.

runs.text: Eu direi hum dito, ou hũa inuenção minha.

lines.note: The translation is that the speaker will offer a saying or an invention of their own. Both hum and the nasal abbreviation hũa preserve the printed forms.
Another Sacu sense is a sowing or crop. Nouidade here means the agricultural yield, not news; the example begins the divided word Cotoxino.
The alternatives describe this year's crop as good or bad. Yoi and varui are linked by l, while the Portuguese translation divides nouidade across the margin.

runs.text: dade deſte anno boa, ou ruim. ¶ Item, O-

lines.note: The crop example concludes with a good or poor harvest this year. A new paragraph introduces the sense of a work or something made, with Obra divided as O-/bra.
Sacu is also a work or creation. Coreua miga ſacugia begins an example asserting that something is the speaker's work; the visible division is retained.

runs.text: Iſto he obra minha, ou feito por minha

lines.note: Gia completes the Japanese assertion. The translation says that the object is the speaker's own work or was made by the speaker's hand.
The first gloss ends with mão, then Deusnogoſacu illustrates God's work. The Japanese phrase incorporates Deus but is a standalone example, not an embedded term in Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Tranqueira, ou cerca que ſe faz de pao

lines.note: A distinct Sacu entry denotes a wooden palisade or enclosure. The material is explicitly timber, and its defensive placement follows below.

runs.text: ao derredor da fortaleza, ou de outro lugar.

lines.note: The wooden barrier surrounds a fortress or another place. This completes the first enclosure sense before the construction example and river-barrier extension.
The example describes constructing a palisade around a place. The Portuguese abbreviation and division trã-/queira are retained, without expanding the nasal mark.

runs.text: queira, ou cerca em torno. ¶ Item, Esta-

lines.note: The first example ends with making the surrounding enclosure. A new sense begins a stake barrier, divided as Esta-/cada at the margin.

runs.text: cada que ſe faz nos rios pera não deixar paßar

lines.note: The stake barrier is built in rivers to prevent passage. A final r is visible in paßar, correcting the truncated paßa of the draft.
The obstruction prevents boats from passing. Sacuuo ſuru illustrates making such a barrier; the translation continues across eſ-/ta.
This completes the example meaning to make the river stake barrier. The short continuation retains both its indentation and the printed physical division.
Sacubo is equated with Qinôno cure, yesterday evening. The Portuguese includes late afternoon and night, with ontem divided across the margin.
The alternative time is yesterday night. This finishes the Portuguese explanation without changing the accent on à or joining the divided ontem.
Sacuban is another expression for yesterday evening or last night. Idem explicitly refers back to the immediately preceding definition.
Sacubiǒ is a feigned illness, explained by the Japanese synonym Tçucuri yamai. The caron over o is retained in the headword.
The example means pretending to be ill. The repeated headword and joined object marker are roman, followed by the concise italic Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Parte dalgũas terras que hum por ſi

lines.note: Sacubun is a portion of land that someone cultivates personally. The last pronoun reads ſi, not the draft's ſe, matching the visible narrow final letter.
The activities are cultivating or sowing that portion of land. This finishes the definition without adding any unstated legal or ownership condition.
Sacuchǒ means yesterday morning. Qinôno is one word despite the large capital Q; the final Portuguese word has two a types with the tilde on the last, and no extra final s is retained.
Sacufan is a half share of the crop. Nouidade has its agricultural sense, and the Japanese example begins a statement about working a rice field on shares.
The example means cultivating the paddy field on a half-share basis. The older Portuguese de meas is preserved, and the running text ends before the separate catchword.
The separate lower-right Sacu- is a catchword, not another body entry. The scan has u and a raised terminal hyphen, correcting the draft’s Saco.
